title: Sanballat, Tobiah and Geshem
lead: The three leaders who opposed Nehemiah's rebuilding of Jerusalem: Sanballat, governor of Samaria; Tobiah, an official of Ammonite origin with family ties in Jerusalem; and Geshem, a king of the Arabs of Qedar. All three are known, or probably known, from sources outside the Bible, and readers debate whether to see them as enemies of God's people or as rival leaders defending their own interests.

sections.b: Sanballat bears a Babylonian name, Sin-uballit ("the moon god Sin has given life"), but named his sons Delaiah and Shelemiah, names honoring the LORD. An Aramaic letter from the Jewish colony at Elephantine in Egypt, dated 407 BC, mentions "Delaiah and Shelemiah, sons of Sanballat, governor of Samaria." "The Horonite" may point to Beth-horon or to Horonaim in Moab. Tobiah also bears a name honoring the LORD; his son married into a leading Jerusalem family and the high priest gave him a room in the Temple (Nehemiah 6:17–19; Nehemiah 13:4–9). A family of Tobiads ruled east of the Jordan for centuries; their name is carved on rock-cut halls at 'Araq el-Emir in Jordan, in letters that scholars date anywhere from the 500s to about 200 BC, and the Zenon papyri (259 BC) mention a Tobiah in Ammon. Geshem (also Gashmu) is probably the "Gashm" or "Geshem" named on an inscribed silver bowl from Tell el-Maskhuta in Egypt, dedicated by "Qaynu son of Geshem, king of Qedar," and in an inscription from Dedan in Arabia. Qedar's kings controlled the incense trade routes south of Judah.

sections.b: The name stayed in the governing family of Samaria. Papyri found in a cave at Wadi Daliyeh, near Jericho, left by refugees from Samaria about 332 BC, include a seal impression of "[...]iah son of Sanballat, governor of Samaria," from the 300s BC. Frank Moore Cross argued from these finds that the family named sons after grandfathers, so that there were two or three governors called Sanballat. Josephus tells of a Sanballat in the time of Alexander the Great whose daughter married Manasseh, brother of the high priest Jaddua, and who built a temple for him on Mount Gerizim (Antiquities 11.302–312). That story looks much like Nehemiah 13:28, where a grandson of the high priest Eliashib marries Sanballat's daughter. Some think Josephus has moved Nehemiah's story a century later; others think the same kind of marriage happened twice in one family.

Read with the memoir, as most Jewish and Christian readers have done, the three are enemies of God's work, and their mockery, plots and hired prophets show how hard faithfulness can be. Many historians add that they were the established leaders of the neighboring provinces and peoples, linked to Jerusalem by marriage and trade, who had real reasons to fear a strong, walled Jerusalem under a governor with the king's backing. On this reading the conflict was also political: Nehemiah's "you have no share in Jerusalem" (Nehemiah 2:20) drew a line that they had not accepted. The two views can stand together, but the memoir tells only Nehemiah's side.
